section_summary: This section documents foreign shipments of arms, ammunition, chemicals, vehicles, machinery, and strategic raw materials connected with Japan’s military expansion from 1932 into 1934. It includes reports from Germany, Britain, China, Peru, and the United States, with especially detailed investigations of Japanese antimony purchases through concealed or indirect trade routes. The section also covers Japanese opposition to President Hoover’s disarmament proposal, domestic munitions production, and preparations to mobilize petroleum, trucks, and foreign-owned factories for wider military operations.

subfiles.title: Continuation: Communist reporting on German war-material exports
subfiles.about: The document assesses Communist newspaper disclosures about alleged German war-material shipments to the Far East.
subfiles.summary: A nationalist newspaper characterizes Communist worker reporting and dock photography as espionage and treason while denying that Germany has an armaments industry. The American consul observes that some Communist disclosures contain identifiable shipping details and appear partly corroborated, although the Communist press probably exaggerates the scale of the trade for political purposes.

subfiles.title: Shipments of War Material via Hamburg to the Far East
subfiles.doc_type: consular despatch with translated newspaper enclosures
subfiles.from: John E. Kohl, American Consul General, Hamburg
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards Communist newspaper reports of German firms allegedly producing chemicals, weapons, and other supplies for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kohl encloses translations from the Hamburger Volkszeitung and photographs purporting to show war shipments at Hamburg. The articles identify barbed wire, ammonia, coke, nitrogen, guns, fuses, pistols, machine-gun parts, and military rifles allegedly destined for Japan or other armament manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Favorable Conditions for War Profiteers
subfiles.doc_type: consular despatch with newspaper article and translation
subfiles.from: Paul J. Gray, American Vice Consul, Stuttgart
subfiles.about: The despatch transmits a Communist report alleging intensified chemical production for explosives at Mannheim-Wohlgelegen.
subfiles.summary: The Süddeutsche Arbeiter-Zeitung claimed that an I.G. Farben-affiliated plant was operating three shifts and new furnaces to produce sodium sulfate for explosives. Its photograph allegedly showed barrels routed through Ludwigshafen to Hankow, and the article called on workers to form control committees and attend an anti-war conference.

subfiles.title: War Material Exported to Japan
subfiles.from: Ray Atherton, Counselor of Embassy, London
subfiles.about: The embassy forwards a House of Commons statement listing British export permits for war material intended for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Hansard extract answers Rhys Davies’s question about permits issued from November 1931 through April 1932. It lists rifle and machine-gun ammunition, machine guns, projectiles, depth-charge equipment, aircraft mountings, armored vehicles, and 40-millimeter guns and ammunition, while withholding monetary values.

subfiles.title: Japanese Purchases of War Materials in Germany
subfiles.doc_type: military intelligence report and distribution sheet
subfiles.from: Hugh W. Rowan, Assistant Military Attaché; forwarded by Jacob W. S. Wuest
subfiles.to: State Department, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The report states that current information on Japanese war-material purchases in Germany shows no important change.
subfiles.summary: Military Intelligence characterizes the latest information as similar in type and source to earlier reporting. Because it shows no alteration in the general situation, the assistant military attaché declines to repeat the details.

subfiles.title: Shipments of War Supplies from Germany to Japan
subfiles.from: Hayne Ellis, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.to: State Department and Military Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The memorandum compiles detailed intelligence about German and Central European shipments of munitions and strategic supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source reports ammunition, dynamite, ammonia, bandages, gun parts, overcoats, sandbags, sulfur, artillery, and nitrate moving through Bremen, Hamburg, Switzerland, Czechoslovakia, and other routes toward Japan. The report also describes Japanese officers observing Krupp gun tests and Soviet shipping officials’ belief that Japan intended eventually to advance from Manchuria toward Vladivostok.

subfiles.title: Scrap-Iron Sales to the Japanese Government
subfiles.from: Director, Division of Investigation, Department of Justice
subfiles.about: The Justice Department forwards a report that Wilmington junk dealers sold ten or fifteen carloads of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Special Deputy Sheriff A. A. McAdams reported learning of the recent sales by two Wilmington dealers. The information was sent to the State Department and also communicated to the Office of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese Attitude Toward the President’s Disarmament Proposals
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to a report on Japanese opposition to President Hoover’s disarmament plan.
subfiles.summary: It notes that the Supreme Military Council reportedly decided to oppose the proposal unconditionally. It summarizes opposition based on hostility to disarmament, Japan’s claimed special position, technical objections, lack of advantage to Japan, and miscellaneous grounds.

subfiles.title: Reaction in Japan to President Hoover’s Disarmament Proposal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch surveys Japanese governmental, military, press, and public opposition to Hoover’s proposal for a one-third reduction in armaments.
subfiles.summary: Grew classifies opposition into five categories, including general dislike of disarmament, Japan’s position beside China and the Soviet Union, technical military objections, financial disadvantages, and broader political arguments. Army and Navy views emphasized Manchuria, manpower, submarines, treaty ratios, and the belief that uniform cuts favored stronger naval powers. An appended Navy Department response rejected drastic proportional reductions and defended an independent Japanese position on submarines.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: British Arms Export Licensing for China and Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a despatch on British regulations governing licenses for munitions exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch discusses the Board of Trade leaflet entitled “The Arms Export Prohibition Order, 1931.” The present page contains only the filing reference and subject description.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Licensed Arms Shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Commission on International Justice and Goodwill, Van Kirk
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to an inquiry about arms shipments to Japan licensed by the United States government.
subfiles.summary: Van Kirk asked whether a New York newspaper editorial describing licensed shipments since the Manchurian episode was correct. The substantive correspondence is filed under another decimal number.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Franklin Engines or Vehicles for the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to correspondence about a possible sale of Franklin engines or vehicles to the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: The proposed transaction involved Frazar and Company, agents in Japan for the Franklin Automobile Company. The referenced file also contains an outline of the War Department’s proposed reply.

subfiles.title: Note on Japanese Army Budget and Military-Supply Production
subfiles.about: The memorandum extracts one significant budget figure from a Military Intelligence report on Japanese military production.
subfiles.summary: The division judged most of the September 22 report to be outside its immediate interest. It retained the press estimate that Japan’s army budget for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1933, would be about 550 million yen, more than twice the current budget.

subfiles.title: Japanese Production of Military Supplies
subfiles.about: The report summarizes Japanese purchases and production of shells, aircraft, tanks, armored cars, trucks, and communications equipment.
subfiles.summary: Sources reported unusually large Army and Navy purchases of sewing machinery, expanded shell production, and substantial output or orders at Japanese aircraft manufacturers. The report also discusses Mitsubishi tank production or assembly at Ōmori and Nagoya, armored-car chassis, military trucks, and proposed radio links, although portions of the OCR are badly garbled.

subfiles.title: Japanese Purchase of Aircraft Material
subfiles.from: Edward F. Witsell, Far Eastern Section, G-2
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports Japanese negotiations to purchase two Boeing aircraft types.
subfiles.summary: Naval Intelligence learned from the U.S. naval material inspector at Boeing in Seattle that the Japanese government was negotiating for a new twin-engine transport. Japan was also interested in an Army Y1B-9A bomber type.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese Purchases of Antimony Regulus
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister at Peiping, relaying the American Consul General at Hankow
subfiles.about: The telegram reports an unprecedented increase in secret Japanese purchases of Chinese antimony regulus.
subfiles.summary: Chinese and German exporters estimated that Japan’s monthly receipts had risen from a normal 135 long tons to about 400 tons. They believed much of the material traveled through Hong Kong and other indirect routes and that the accumulation was intended for greatly increased munitions production.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Inform Tokyo of the Antimony Report
subfiles.about: The Department directs the legation to send the information on Japanese antimony purchases to Tokyo by mail.
subfiles.summary: The brief telegram responds to Peiping’s November 20 message. It contains only the instruction to inform Tokyo and the associated communications markings.

subfiles.title: Departmental Summary of Hankow’s Antimony Report
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes evidence that Japan was secretly obtaining more than 400 tons of antimony regulus per month for munitions.
subfiles.summary: The note compares the claimed Japanese purchases with the normal monthly requirement and with the unexplained rise in exports to “other countries.” It attributes secrecy to efforts to avoid suspicion and defeat the Chinese boycott, and recounts an attempted 500-ton purchase by a Japanese naval officer through a British brokerage firm.

subfiles.title: Japanese Purchases of Antimony
subfiles.from: Reginald P. Mitchell, American Vice Consul, Hankow; approved by Walter A. Adams
subfiles.about: The report investigates the scale, purpose, and concealed routes of Japanese antimony-regulus purchases in China.
subfiles.summary: Exporters estimated that Japan was acquiring more than 400 long tons monthly against a normal requirement of about 135 tons and believed the surplus was for munitions. Customs tables showed rising direct exports to Japan and a striking increase under “Other Countries,” much of which dealers traced to Hong Kong or other indirect Far Eastern routes. T. Y. Li described the Chinese boycott and a failed effort by a Japanese naval officer to obtain 500 tons through a British intermediary.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: French Arms Exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram reporting Chinese press claims that French arms exports to Japan had increased sixfold.
subfiles.summary: The comparison begins with Japan’s occupation of Manchuria in September 1931. The underlying telegram appears on the following page and is also indexed under another decimal classification.

subfiles.title: Chinese Press Criticism of French Arms Exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister at Peiping, relaying Nanking
subfiles.about: The telegram reports Chinese press accusations that French arms exports to Japan had risen sixfold since the occupation of Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Chinese newspapers denounced France for materially assisting Japanese military aggression in China. They stressed the inconsistency between that trade and France’s position as a League of Nations member and professed friend of China.

subfiles.title: Japanese Purchases of Antimony Regulus
subfiles.doc_type: consular trade report with statistical enclosure
subfiles.from: Richard P. Butrick, American Consul, Shanghai
subfiles.about: The report supplements Hankow’s investigation with interviews and statistics concerning direct and indirect Japanese antimony purchases.
subfiles.summary: Shanghai dealers believed that Japan was buying more antimony than its depressed civilian industries could consume and was routing cargo through Great Britain, nearby Asian ports, and other nominal destinations. The report compares Chinese customs figures across countries and years, examines discrepancies with American consular declarations, and notes purchases in Europe. It also recounts a disguised Japanese purchase of zinc ore near Hankow whose vessel was redirected after clearing Wusong.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Increased Japanese Munitions Activity
subfiles.about: The telegram reports increased Japanese production of munitions and purchases of machinery and strategic raw materials abroad.
subfiles.summary: The military attaché’s latest survey found that Japanese Army procurement and domestic munitions manufacture had expanded. The message is brief and supplies no itemized figures or commodities.

subfiles.title: Letter Concerning Nitrate and Scrap-Iron Shipments
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Thomas asks the State Department to act against American nitrate and scrap-iron shipments that might aid Japan’s war preparations.
subfiles.summary: Thomas encloses a January 19 Norfolk newspaper article about the cargoes. He warns that American materials could eventually be used against the American fleet and soldiers.

subfiles.title: Japanese Vessels Get Nitrates in Local Port
subfiles.to: Enclosure to W. H. Thomas’s letter
subfiles.about: The clipping reports Japanese ships loading nitrates at Hopewell and scrap iron at Norfolk-area terminals.
subfiles.summary: It states that five Japanese ships had recently sailed, one carrying 3,503 tons, and observes that atmospheric nitrate and scrap iron can be used in munitions. Unrelated columns on the same newspaper page mention Senate debate, Babe Ruth, and Kid Chocolate.

subfiles.title: Reply to W. H. Thomas
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Thomas’s letter and clipping about nitrate and scrap-iron shipments to the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks Thomas for his interest and courtesy in forwarding the article. The reply makes no commitment to restrict or investigate the shipments.

subfiles.title: Routing Sheet for the Peru Strategic-Minerals Report
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence and Military Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The sheet records departmental circulation of information about possible Japanese mineral purchases in Peru.
subfiles.summary: It indicates distribution to naval and military intelligence and coordination with Latin American affairs. The page contains routing marks rather than substantive evidence.

subfiles.title: Summary of Reported Japanese Interest in Peruvian Minerals
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a report that a Yokohama trading company sought Peruvian strategic minerals because Japan expected war.
subfiles.summary: An American engineer had seen a translated letter obtained by a Peruvian miner through an employee of a Japanese firm. The alleged letter sought vanadium substitutes, tungsten, scheelite, and molybdenite, although no important international shipments from Peru appeared in customs publications.

subfiles.title: Prospective Purchase of Minerals in Peru by the Japanese Government
subfiles.about: The report records evidence that Japanese interests were investigating Peruvian sources of strategic metals for war production.
subfiles.summary: Henry James Parks said that miner Luis Delgado had shown him a translation of a Japanese letter obtained through the firm of Shakichi Tokada. The Pacific Trading Company of Yokohama allegedly stated that war was certain and requested tungsten, scheelite, and molybdenite for gunmetal and hardened steel. Parks confirmed that the minerals existed in Peru but knew of no significant international shipments.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Aviation Supplies and Equipment for Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a letter about shipment of aviation supplies and equipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The substantive letter is filed under decimal number 861.24/344. This page supplies only the sender, date, subject, and cross-reference.

subfiles.title: Summary of Stuttgart Despatch on Intensified War-Material Shipments
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Communist report of intensified shipments of war material from Hamburg to Japan.
subfiles.summary: It identifies Stuttgart despatch number 871 of January 24, 1933, as the source. The underlying despatch follows on pages 147–148.

subfiles.title: Shipment of War Material to Japan
subfiles.from: Leon Dominian, American Consul General in Charge, Stuttgart
subfiles.about: The despatch relays a Communist newspaper report of artillery, powder, and other military cargoes moving from Hamburg toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Süddeutsche Arbeiter-Zeitung alleged that the Japanese steamer Konlia Maru was loading artillery and that the British steamer Hermin regularly carried powder for transshipment to Japanese vessels. It also named Rickmers and Norddeutscher Lloyd ships said to be loading or carrying war material from Schulauer Hafen and Brunshausen to Japanese destinations.

subfiles.title: Routing Notation on the Naval Intelligence Commendation
subfiles.about: The page contains internal routing and action notations associated with Naval Intelligence’s praise for the Hankow antimony reports.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text is fragmentary and principally administrative. It appears to ask whether an appropriate instruction or acknowledgment should be issued.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence Appreciation of Reginald P. Mitchell’s Reports
subfiles.from: Hayne Ellis, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Ellis commends two Hankow reports by Vice Consul Reginald P. Mitchell and asks that the author be informed of their value.
subfiles.summary: The reports praised are “Review of Antimony Market” and “Japanese Purchases of Antimony.” Ellis describes them as careful, conscientious, invaluable, and appreciated by the Office of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to the Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Hayne Ellis, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Ellis’s commendation of Mitchell’s Hankow antimony reports.
subfiles.summary: The letter thanks Ellis for his appreciation of the reports dated October 20 and November 18, 1932. It identifies Vice Consul Reginald P. Mitchell as their author.

subfiles.title: Instruction Forwarding Naval Intelligence’s Commendation
subfiles.about: The Department forwards Ellis’s complimentary letter concerning Mitchell’s two antimony reports.
subfiles.summary: The instruction notes the Department’s gratification at Naval Intelligence’s commendatory remarks. It encloses the February 7 letter and identifies the two reports prepared by Mitchell.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Possible Military Use of the Ford Plant in Japan
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum highlights a commercial attaché’s report that Japan might requisition Ford’s Japanese works for war production.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Military Ordnance Depot reportedly told Ford that its plant could be used to manufacture war material during the April 1933–March 1934 fiscal year. Hornbeck notes that the commercial attaché said the ambassador had been fully informed, although the State Department had received nothing from him on the matter.

subfiles.title: Use of American-Owned Factories by the Japanese Military
subfiles.to: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: The report quotes a Japanese military notice concerning wartime use of Ford’s Japanese plant and its employees.
subfiles.summary: The Imperial Japanese Government’s Military Ordnance Depot stated that Ford’s works could be operated for military purposes under the Munitions Industries Mobilization Law if war required it. Ford was also instructed to investigate employees seeking leave for military service and to keep the matter strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Arms Embargo for the Far East
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Secretary Stimson’s discussion with the Belgian ambassador about an arms embargo in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Stimson emphasized the moral judgment delivered by forty-two nations on the Far Eastern situation. He argued for deliberation before linking that judgment to an arms measure that would have little effect on Japan because Japan manufactured most of its own arms.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese Mobilization of Resources
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram indicating Japanese preparations for possible resource mobilization and wider military operations.
subfiles.summary: It identifies Tokyo telegram number 59 as the relevant document. The telegram itself appears on the next page and is cross-filed under another decimal classification.

subfiles.title: Japanese Survey and Mobilization of Petroleum and Trucks
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The telegram reports Japanese inquiries into oil-company imports and requisition of subsidized commercial trucks for Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Japanese authorities ordered Standard Oil and Rising Sun Petroleum to report past and projected imports through June, an unprecedented request according to Standard Oil’s manager. The War Office was also requisitioning subsidized commercial trucks to carry supplies to army units in Manchuria. Grew found no definite connection between the measures but interpreted them as evidence of a survey or possible mobilization for more extensive operations.

subfiles.title: Note on Interdepartmental Acknowledgments
subfiles.about: The note records an understanding that correspondence between departments is not acknowledged unless confirmation of receipt is necessary.
subfiles.summary: The writer states that an interdepartmental arrangement dispenses with routine acknowledgments. The writer nevertheless confirmed that understanding; no specific underlying letter is identified on the page.
